CEDiR’s aim is to consolidate and extend this research, reaching across disciplines and contexts to develop the potential of educational dialogue at all education levels and to have an impact on theory, policy and practice. More about our aims and perspectives is summarised in the CEDiR Working Paper , collaboratively written by many of the group's members as a dialogue. CEDiR members represent a range of Faculty colleagues, drawn together through a common interest in dialogic education. The group seeks to promote collaboration and develop capacity at all levels, with a focus on supporting postgraduate students and early career staff. CEDiR is forging links with senior academics and practitioners in the field worldwide and already has a substantial number of high profile international collaborators and associates. Its main priority is on creating a supportive environment for creating and sharing high quality research that will shape the future of education. Please take a look at our upcoming CEDiR events . For queries email cedir @ educ.cam.ac.uk . CEDiR Research Strands CEDiR has several inter-connected Research Strands . These build on existing work undertaken by the Faculty of Education to consider important contemporary topics relating to dialogic education. Research undertaken includes every level of education from early years to HE, professional dialogues, and other dialogue outside of classrooms. Multimodal dialogue Dialogue, professional change and leadership Digital technology and dialogue Classroom dialogue and practitioner inquiry CEDiR Projects Examples of current/recent projects undertaken by CEDiR colleagues include: Talking Objects Toolkit for Systematic Educational Dialogue Analysis (T-SEDA) DIalogue and Argumentation for Cultural Literacy Learning in Schools (DIALLS) Digitalised Dialogues Across the Curriculum (DiDiAC) ED:TALK – Evidence & Dialogue Toolkit Thinking Together Virtual Internships Project (VIP) CEDiR Members The group is led by Sara Hennessy . The CEDiR steering group also includes Imogen Casebourne , Emma Cooper , Riikka Hofmann and Alison Twiner . PhD students Xinyue Zhou, Bill Bradley, Nunu Zheng and Stacy Marshall support CEDiR's communications and community activities. See the full list of members and our collaborators and associates . Accept and close View privacy policy Home About Map & How To Reach Us Green Impact and Sustainability Visiting Scholars Visiting Students Study with Us Undergraduate Study PGCE Study Postgraduate Study Practitioner Professional Development Counselling Student Engagement & Feedback Research About our research Research Groups and Centres Research Programmes Impact Events Cambridge Journal of Education Networks & Innovation CRiCLE Network NRICH mathematics Cambridge School Classics Project CIAN Network Leadership for Learning SUPER Network Cambridge Primary Review Trust People Academic Staff Emeritus Readers and Professors Doctoral Students Equality and Diversity News News Statements Media enquiries Events Open Research Seminar calendar Conferences Recorded seminars and lectures Library Faculty Library - home Your Library Guides - Moodle site Library Blog - FYI Opening Hours Services COVID-19 guidance Remote working guide IT Service Booker - Book a room Moodle VLE Office 365 Google Apps@Cambridge External Bookings educ NET Vacancies About Us Faculty of Education Research Research Groups and Centres CEDiR: Cambridge Educational Dialogue Research About Us About our research Research Groups Research Programmes Impact Events Cambridge Journal of Education There is a growing global movement of research focussing on the potential of dialogue in transforming education. Dialogue is a complex concept; it draws on many different traditions, beginning with Socrates and Plato, and including Dewey, Freire, Buber and Bakhtin as well as more recent authors (Alexander, Boyd, Clarke, Hennessy, Mercer, Michaels, O’Connor, Resnick, Rojas-Drummond, Scott, Šedova, Wegerif, Wells, etc.). There is considerable variation in focus within the field, with some authors using the term synonymously with talk or discourse while others take more focused theoretical approaches. While our initial position is open to adaptation and debate by researchers in the group, we currently understand ‘dialogue’ as follows (building on sociocultural and dialogic theories, especially Bakhtin and Vygotsky): Dialogue is intelligible both as a pedagogical tool for subject teaching and learning, and as an end in itself – linked to what is increasingly referred to as ‘future education’ meaning education for critical and higher level thinking, creative problem solving, democratic citizenship and living peacefully on an increasingly interconnected planet. Dialogue is the continuous co-construction of new meanings that emerge through the dialogic space that opens up out of the gap between different perspectives. Dialogicality is a quality of communication not limited to talk; it can also be found in non-verbal human communication and multimodal forms of dialogue, interaction with text (multimodal and traditional written forms), and interaction with digital artefacts. Dialogue is intrinsically challenging and logistically and ideologically constrained by the prevailing educational discourse, curriculum and assessment frameworks, together posing stimulating questions for researchers and practitioners. The dialogic education movement is associated with Cambridge due to seminal work done by Robin Alexander, Neil Mercer , Christine Howe in particular. CEDiR has built and expanded upon this work, growing to become a large and vibrant group. The group has since grown to over 70 Faculty (and wider University) staff and research students , representing a wide range of interests in dialogue. It is led by Sara Hennessy . The CEDiR steering group also includes Imogen Casebourne, Emma Cooper, Riikka Hofmann and Alison Twiner. PhD students Xinyue Zhou, Bill Bradley, Nunu Zheng and Stacy Marshall support the group's communications and community activities. (Sarah Fitri, Mher Davtyan, Yi Zhao, Luwei Bai, Nowsha Farha, Sakina Jafri, Dongkeun Han, Samantha Hulston, Ryan Irvan, Qian Liu, Kevin Martin, Ana Laura Trigo-Clapes, Ana Rubio-Jimenez and Lulu Zhao previously supported CEDiR in this capacity.) Affiliated external members include our current collaborators and associates , alumni , and practitioners involved in dialogue-related research and practice. sources.title: Sherice Clarke
sources.text: Sherice Clarke Associate Professor snclarke@ucsd.edu (858) 246-2594 Profile Education Research Interests/Affiliation Profile Sherice Clarke is an Associate Professor in the Department of Education Studies. Dr. Clarke is a learning scientist who uses microgenetic discourse methodologies to study learning in and out of school. She is currently engaged in research on teacher learning, research-practice partnerships, design-based research, and community design-based research. Before joining the faculty at UC San Diego, she was a postdoctoral fellow and research associate at the University of Pittsburgh’s Learning Research and Development Center. Dr. Clarke received her Ph.D. in Education from the University of Edinburgh’s Moray House School of Education. In 2022, she received the National Science Foundation CAREER Award, the foundation’s most prestigious award supporting early-career faculty. Education PhD in Education University of Edinburgh, Moray House School of Education Master of Education University of Edinburgh, Moray House School of Education BA in Art History City University of New York, Hunter College Research For list of current and previous projects and publications please visit www.shericeclarke.com Interests/Affiliation Interests: educational equity, classroom dialogue, student engagement, teacher cognition, educational technologies Affliation: International Partner – Cambridge Educational Dialogue Research Group
